sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: Prior work has documented multiple mechanisms and manifestations of verbosity/length bias in assistant LLMs, as well as mitigation strategies for length-sensitive evaluation. Verbosity measurement and correlates. Zhang et al. (2025) introduce the verbosity compensation (VC) score, showing that models often answer with more words than necessary even when explicitly instructed to be concise. They demonstrate that VC is pervasive across models and datasets (e.g., GPT-4 shows \approx50% VC frequency on some tasks). They also observe that verbose answers are often less accurate, with large performance gaps between concise and verbose settings, and report that verbosity correlates with uncertainty signals such as higher perplexity and related uncertainty metrics. Length bias in preference learning and LLM-judged evaluation. Shen et al. (2023) investigate length bias in RLHF reward models, showing that vanilla reward models can learn a shortcut where longer responses receive systematically higher scores, even when additional text does not improve helpfulness. Relatedly, when GPT-4 is used as a proxy judge, it tends to favor longer answers over shorter ones at comparable quality ( Saito et al., 2023 ; Dubois et al., 2024 ) , inducing a length-correlated bias that advantages verbose models in win-rate–based evaluations. To address this, Dubois et al. (2024) introduce a length-controlled win rate that removes the length term from the preference regression, improving robustness to verbosity manipulation and increasing correlation with LMSYS Chatbot Arena rankings ( Chiang et al., 2024 ) . Hu et al. (2024) further analyze length bias in LLM-as-a-judge settings by decomposing win rate into length-independent desirability and length-dependent information mass (quantified via conditional entropy), and argue that longer responses gain higher win rates primarily through increased information mass. Building on this view, they introduce AdapAlpaca, a variant of AlpacaEval that dynamically matches the length of reference and test responses to mitigate length bias in automatic preference evaluation. Over-reasoning as a failure mode of over-generation. Chiang and Lee ( Chiang and Lee, 2024 ) study over-reasoning in LLMs using GSM8K-Zero, where questions can be answered directly from the prompt text without any calculations. They show that RLHF-trained models nonetheless produce lengthy, unnecessary chains of calculation on these trivial problems, often introducing errors and lowering accuracy compared to short, direct answers. Using GPT-4 as proxy reward models, they further find that these judges systematically prefer long answers even when the long answer is wrong and a competing short answer is correct-implicating length-favoring preference mechanisms as a driver of redundant reasoning. Reference-free conciseness metrics. Ghafari et al. (2025) show that conciseness is positively correlated with human judgments of redundancy and verbosity across several tasks. They propose ConCISE, a reference-free conciseness metric that estimates redundancy by generating compressed variants of an answer (abstractive, extractive, and pruned) and using an LLM judge to verify semantic and entity preservation. However, this approach requires multiple additional LLM calls, is sensitive to the choice of helper model and prompts, and treats the original answer as the reference rather than anchoring conciseness to task-specific minimal sufficiency or distinguishing brevity-focused from explanation-heavy settings.

sections.heading: 3 YapBench
sections.text: YapBench is a benchmark for measuring user-visible over-generation on brevity-ideal prompts. Each benchmark item is a triple (p_{i},b_{i},c_{i}): a single-turn prompt p_{i}, a short reference baseline b_{i}, and a category label c_{i}. The baseline is the minimal sufficient answer : the shortest response that is still correct, clear, and sufficient for a typical user. The YapBench benchmark asks a question : when a short answer is enough, how much longer does the model answer than this baseline? Informally, YapBench compares assistant LLMs on how much they over-generate (”yap”) beyond a prompt-specific minimal sufficient answer on prompts where brevity is ideal. Formally, YapBench is designed to measure unnecessary verbosity in settings where a short answer is clearly sufficient. The benchmark is built around three goals: 1. Isolation of verbosity. Evaluate verbosity separately from other axes (e.g., correctness, safety), rather than collapsing them into a single scalar. 2. Brevity-ideal scope. Focus core metrics on prompts where annotators broadly agree that short, direct answers are preferred. 3. Practical simplicity. Enable evaluation with standard APIs and offline scoring from logged model outputs.

sections.heading: 3.1 Prompt set and categories
sections.text: We group prompts into a small number of categories to keep analysis interpretable. Different models “yap” for different reasons (e.g., filling the vacuum on nonsense, or adding explanations around a one-line command). For the initial version of the benchmark we selected three prompt categories: Prompt Category A: minimal / ambiguous input. Category A is designed to stress-test assistants on low-information turns, where the safest and most useful behavior is to ask for clarification (or give a minimal acknowledgment), not to guess intent. Concretely, the category includes (i) pure noise inputs with no semantic content (empty/whitespace-only, punctuation spam, keyboard mashes, emoji-only), and (ii) underspecified openers that signal a problem but provide no details (e.g., help , error , fix this , how? , it doesn’t work ). We also include short phatic tokens (e.g., ok , cool , thanks ) and bare digits (e.g., 1 , 42 ) as ambiguous turns that commonly trigger over-interpretation. Baselines therefore use minimal templates: a short clarification request (e.g., Please rephrase. , What do you need help with? ) or a minimal acknowledgment (e.g., OK. , You’re welcome. ). The goal of Category A is to measure how much models over-generate when the prompt is unclear: do they stay minimal, or do they produce extended, unsolicited content despite insufficient context? Prompt Category B: short factual Q&A (closed-form). Category B targets prompts where the user is clearly asking for a single fact and a one-token (or very short) answer is sufficient. The prompts are intentionally closed-form: capitals, simple arithmetic, basic geometry, chemical symbols and formulas, atomic numbers, common biological facts, and canonical authorship/date questions. We also include a small number of “confusion-prone” but still unambiguous items (e.g., What is the capital of Australia? ) to capture a frequent assistant behavior: adding disclaimers or extra context around a straightforward fact. The goal of Category B is to measure over-generation in the simplest information-seeking setting: when the prompt has a unique, stable answer, does the model return the minimal fact, or does it add avoidable explanation and filler? Prompt Category C: one-line coding task / command. Category C targets prompts where the user requests an atomic, one-line output : a shell command, a regex pattern, a simple SQL statement, or a single-line code snippet. The v0.1 set spans common command-line tasks ( wc , find , grep , tar , df , tail ), Git one-liners, basic SQL SELECT/WHERE and aggregates, practical regexes, and short idiomatic snippets in Python/JavaScript/Java/Rust/Docker. Baselines in this category are exactly one line by construction. The goal of Category C is to measure a very common assistant failure mode in technical help: when a single line is sufficient, does the model output only the one-liner, or does it add extra prose (headings, explanations, duplicated code blocks) that increases length without improving task completion? Dataset size (v0.1). YapBench v0.1 contains 304 English prompts: 60 in Category A, 126 in Category B, and 118 in Category C. At the moment of writing the category counts in YapBench are unequal. This does not induce a weighting effect in the aggregate metric: YapIndex is computed from category-level medians and then combined with uniform category weights (Section 3.3 ), so category contribution is not proportional to the number of prompts. The role of |\mathcal{I}_{c}| is primarily statistical: larger categories yield more stable estimates of the category median, rather than systematically shifting the aggregate score. Cat. Description (brevity-ideal) A Nonsense / Minimal Input. Inputs with no actionable semantic content (e.g., punctuation, emoji-only, placeholders for blank input). Ideal behavior is a minimal clarification request or minimal acknowledgment. B Short Factual Q&A. Closed-form questions with a unique, stable answer (e.g., capitals, authorship, basic arithmetic) where a word/number (or short phrase) suffices. C One-line Coding Task/ Command. Atomic operations with a canonical one-line solution (e.g., a shell command, regex, one-line code) where returning the single line is sufficient. Table 2: Core prompt categories in YapBench . Each category targets a common interaction regime where brevity is the appropriate default and over-generation is user-visible. See Section 3.1 for the full category definitions and examples.

sections.heading: 3.2 Minimal sufficient baselines
sections.text: For each prompt p_{i}, we define a baseline b_{i} that represents the minimal sufficient response. Baselines are intentionally short: they are not “best possible” answers, only the minimum needed to satisfy the prompt. Baseline rules (operational). Each (p_{i},b_{i}) pair is curated to satisfy: • Unambiguous intent. The prompt targets one task and one correct answer in standard usage (up to trivial surface variants). • Minimal sufficiency. The baseline is as short as possible while still correct and clear; removing any token should break correctness or clarity. • Atomic and self-contained. No reliance on prior turns or hidden context. • Standard practice. When multiple short correct answers exist, choose the idiomatic/common one (especially in code/commands). • Reproducible. Items that produce disagreement about “minimal sufficient” are revised or removed. How baselines look in each category. • A: a minimal clarification (e.g., Please rephrase. , What do you need help with? ) or a minimal acknowledgment for phatic inputs (e.g., OK. , You’re welcome. ). This is why Category A includes multiple baseline types . • B: a single token or short phrase (e.g., Paris , 12 , H 2 O , Yes ). • C: exactly one line of code, command, or pattern, with no additional symbols (e.g., Markdown formatting). Baseline construction and review. Baselines are written to be minimal rather than exhaustive: the shortest answer that remains correct, clear, and sufficient for a typical user. We iteratively refined (p_{i},b_{i}) pairs using internal review: for each prompt, we edited the baseline down to the shortest form that still preserves correctness and clarity, and removed or rewrote prompts where “minimal sufficient” produced repeated disagreements. This process emphasizes reproducibility: if a prompt does not admit a stable minimal answer under standard usage, it is excluded or corrected in the future versions of the benchamrk.

sections.heading: 3.3 Measures: YapScore, YapIndex, and YapTax
sections.text: In this subsection, we define quantitative measures for unnecessary verbosity on brevity-ideal prompts. The key idea is to measure how much extra text a model produces beyond a prompt-specific minimal sufficient answer. Definition 1 (Per-prompt YapScore (Excess Length)) . Let i\in\mathcal{I} index a prompt with baseline answer length B_{i}\in\mathbb{N}, measured in characters. For a model M, let L_{i}(M)\in\mathbb{N} denote the character length of its response to prompt i. The per-prompt YapScore is defined as \mathrm{YapScore}_{i}(M)\;=\;\max\{0,\;L_{i}(M)-B_{i}\}. (1) Interpretation. \mathrm{YapScore}_{i}(M) measures the number of extra characters generated by model M beyond the minimal sufficient answer for prompt i. A score of zero indicates a baseline-length response. Larger values indicate increasing amounts of unnecessary verbosity. By construction, this metric is robust to extremely short baselines and requires no smoothing or tuning parameters. Definition 2 (Category and Aggregate YapIndex) . Let \mathcal{I}_{c}\subseteq\mathcal{I} denote the set of prompts belonging to category c\in\mathcal{C}, where \mathcal{C} is the set of benchmark categories (e.g., \mathcal{C}=\{A,B,C\}). The category-level YapIndex is defined as Y_{c}(M)\;=\;\operatorname{median}\{\mathrm{YapScore}_{i}(M):i\in\mathcal{I}_{c}\}. (2) The aggregate YapIndex is the weighted average of category indices: \mathrm{YapIndex}(M)\;=\;\sum_{c\in\mathcal{C}}w_{c}\,Y_{c}(M), (3) where w_{c}\geq 0 are category weights with \sum_{c\in\mathcal{C}}w_{c}=1 (uniform by default). Aggregation Rationale. We use the median within each category to reduce sensitivity to rare extreme verbosity bursts and to avoid dominance by prompts with very short baselines. Aggregating across categories ensures that the final YapIndex reflects verbosity behavior across distinct interaction regimes rather than a single prompt type. Why are baselines required? Verbosity is inherently relative to task sufficiency. The baseline B_{i} defines the minimum information required to correctly and clearly answer prompt i. Without baselines, a length-based metric would conflate necessary content with unnecessary over-generation and would reduce to measuring response length rather than unnecessary verbosity.

sections.heading: 3.3.1 Uncertainty estimation (bootstrap confidence intervals)
sections.text: Since YapBench reports medians of heavy-tailed excess-length distributions, we estimate uncertainty using a nonparametric bootstrap over prompts (percentile intervals). For each model and each statistic reported, we run B=1000 bootstrap iterations. Each iteration resamples prompts with replacement and recomputes the statistic on the resampled set. Category medians. For a category c\in\{A,B,C\} with per-prompt YapScores \{s_{i}\}_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{c}}, bootstrap iteration b draws a resample \{s^{*(b)}_{j}\}_{j=1}^{|\mathcal{I}_{c}|} and computes the bootstrap median m_{c}^{(b)}\;=\;\operatorname{median}\!\left(\{s^{*(b)}_{j}\}_{j=1}^{|\mathcal{I}_{c}|}\right). (4) We form a 95% percentile confidence interval for the category median as [L_{c},U_{c}]\;=\;\left[Q_{0.025}\!\left(\{m_{c}^{(b)}\}_{b=1}^{B}\right),\;Q_{0.975}\!\left(\{m_{c}^{(b)}\}_{b=1}^{B}\right)\right]. (5) YapIndex. To capture uncertainty in the aggregate score, each bootstrap iteration resamples within each category and recomputes the full index: \displaystyle m_{c}^{(b)} \displaystyle\leftarrow\operatorname{median}\!\left(\text{resample of Cat\penalty\ }c\text{ scores}\right),\hskip 20.00003ptc\in\{A,B,C\}, (6) \displaystyle\mathrm{YapIndex}^{(b)} \displaystyle=\sum_{c\in\{A,B,C\}}w_{c}\,m_{c}^{(b)}. We then take the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of \{\mathrm{YapIndex}^{(b)}\}_{b=1}^{B} to obtain the 95% percentile interval [L,U]. Reporting as a half-width. For compact presentation, we summarize each 95% interval [L,U] by its half-width \Delta_{95}\;=\;\frac{U-L}{2}, (7) and report statistics as \hat{s}\pm\Delta_{95}. Note that bootstrap percentile intervals for medians can be asymmetric; the \pm notation is a symmetric summary intended to ease comparison across models. (Uniform w_{c} is used by default.)

sections.heading: 3.3.2 Cost-based measure: YapTax
sections.text: While YapScore is computed in characters for tokenizer-agnostic comparison, we also report a cost-oriented secondary metric that estimates the marginal dollar cost of over-generation under token-based pricing. Definition 3 (Excess output tokens) . Let T_{i}(M)\in\mathbb{N} denote the number of output tokens produced by model M on prompt i, and let T_{i}(b) denote the number of tokens in the minimal sufficient baseline b_{i}, computed under a fixed tokenizer. We define excess output tokens as \mathrm{ExcessTok}_{i}(M)\;=\;\max\{0,\;T_{i}(M)-T_{i}(b)\}. (8) Definition 4 (Per-prompt YapTax (USD)) . Let p_{M} be the output-token price for model M in USD per token. The per-prompt YapTax is defined as \mathrm{YapTax}_{i}(M)\;=\;\mathrm{ExcessTok}_{i}(M)\cdot p_{M}. (9) Definition 5 (Aggregate YapTax per 1,000 prompts) . For a set of evaluated prompts \mathcal{I} with |\mathcal{I}|=N, we report \mathrm{YapTax}_{\$1000}(M)\;=\;1000\cdot\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}}\mathrm{YapTax}_{i}(M). (10) Interpretation. \mathrm{YapTax}_{\$1000}(M) is the expected additional dollar cost attributable to over-generation for 1,000 benchmark queries under the model’s output-token pricing. Implementation details. • T_{i}(M) uses the model’s non-reasoning output tokens (excluding chain-of-thought tokens when reported separately by the API). • T_{i}(b) is computed by tokenizing b_{i} using each model’s own tokenizer. • Output-token prices p_{M} are retrieved from the OpenRouter API 1 1 1 https://openrouter.ai at 31.12.2025. sections.heading: 4 Evaluation Protocol and Parameters
sections.text: Access, prompting, and decoding. All models are queried via the OpenRouter API with absent system prompt. We set temperature to 0 whenever the model endpoint exposes this control; for endpoints that do not allow temperature configuration (e.g., GPT-5 variants), we use the provider default, the rest of hyperparameters are default to each provider. All prompts are evaluated independently in a single-turn setting with no prior context. Length units. The primary YapScore is computed in characters to enable tokenizer-agnostic comparison across providers. We also neglect the markdown characters from the YapScore calculations. Correctness and sufficiency. YapBench v0.1 is intentionally constructed so that Category B (closed-form factual items) and Category C (atomic one-line commands/snippets) are trivial to answer correctly for essentially any instruction-tuned model. Consequently, we do not apply an explicit correctness gate in the main results; the benchmark is designed to isolate over-generation behavior rather than task difficulty. Category A items are likewise evaluated primarily for verbosity behavior on underspecified inputs, where the desired behavior is a minimal clarification or acknowledgment rather than substantive content. Reasoning-model ablations. For models that expose explicit “reasoning” modes or verbosity controls, we run paired evaluations with these features enabled and disabled to measure their impact on YapScore and category-level behavior. Importantly, YapScore is computed only from the user-visible final answer : we exclude any hidden or separately reported reasoning traces (e.g., chain-of-thought tokens) from length and token counts whenever the API provides them separately.

sections.heading: 5 Results
sections.text: We evaluate models using the excess-length YapScore and the aggregate YapIndex defined in Section 3.3 . All results report median excess characters beyond the minimal sufficient baseline, aggregated across prompt categories with uniform weights.

sections.heading: 5.3 Results: Category-Level Behavior
sections.text: Category medians reveal distinct verbosity failure modes: Category A (underspecified / ambiguous inputs). Category A can be a major source of excess length: several models generate large median overhead on low-information prompts, consistent with a tendency to “fill the vacuum” with unsolicited content rather than issuing a minimal clarification. Category B (short factual Q&A). Median excess in Category B is low for some models but dominates for others, especially on confusion-prone yet closed-form questions, indicating that many assistants add avoidable context or caveats even when a single fact is sufficient. Category C (one-line code tasks). Category C frequently drives the largest median excess for many models, reflecting formatting and explanation overhead (e.g., headings, prose, or duplicated code blocks) around atomic commands or snippets where a one-line answer would suffice. Lastly, while YapIndex summarizes typical behavior via medians, over-generation can be highly variable across prompts; we therefore complement median-based reporting with tail statistics (e.g., percentiles) to characterize worst-case “verbosity bursts” that are most disruptive for user experience and cost. Figure 1: Example of user-visible over-generation on a brevity-ideal prompt (Category B: closed-form factual Q&A). The prompt ( “What is the largest planet in our solar system?” ) has a unique, stable, one-word answer, and the minimal sufficient baseline for YapBench is simply “Jupiter” The figure shows four assistant-style LLM responses to the same query: GPT-3.5-Turbo matches the baseline with a single-token reply, while Claude-Sonnet-4.5 , Gemini-3-Pro , and DeepSeek-v3.2 expand the response with additional (correct) context such as diameter unit conversions, relative size/mass comparisons, bullet-point formatting, and summary statements. Although these longer outputs are factually consistent, they are unnecessary for sufficiency given the user’s closed-form request, increasing reading and scrolling burden and inflating token-based inference cost.

sections.heading: 6 Discussion
sections.text: Brevity-optimal behavior is not aligned with model recency or perceived capability. A central finding of YapBench is that response verbosity on brevity-ideal prompts is not monotonic in model generation or perceived frontier capability. In particular, a model from 2023 gpt-3.5-turbo achieves the best overall YapIndex (23) in our evaluation (Table 4 ), outperforming a range of newer frontier assistant models (Gemini-Pro, GPT-5, etc). This result suggests that unnecessary verbosity is not an inherent consequence of scale or general competence. Instead, it appears to be a behavioral property that is influenced by post-training and assistant-style response priors. From a deployment perspective, this decoupling implies that selecting models solely based on conventional capability benchmarks can yield suboptimal user experience and higher inference cost in brevity-ideal settings. Verbosity is heterogeneous across interaction regimes, motivating category-level analysis. YapBench was designed to separate distinct regimes where brevity is typically preferred, and the results confirm that models exhibit markedly different behavior across categories. The category leaderboards (Table 5 ) show that some models can be near-minimal on closed-form factual queries (Category B), while simultaneously producing substantial over-generation on underspecified inputs (Category A) or one-line technical coding requests (Category C). This heterogeneity indicates that a single global verbosity score is insufficient to characterize assistant behavior in practice. Reporting category-level outcomes is therefore essential to identify which interaction types drive excess length and to diagnose failure modes that are likely to be product-critical. Underspecified inputs bring out systematic over-generation that is better explained as a policy prior than a knowledge limitation. Category A prompts contain low-information turns for which the minimal sufficient behavior is a short clarification request or acknowledgment. Despite the absence of actionable task information, many models generate extended content, which we interpret as a systematic tendency to produce proactive, generic assistance rather than requesting missing context. Because Category A baselines are intentionally minimal, excess length in this regime directly quantifies an assistant prior to respond substantively even when the prompt does not support it. This behavior is particularly salient from a human factors and cost perspective, since so-called ”vacuum-filling” responses can become long while providing limited incremental utility. One-line technical requests expose formatting and explanation overhead as a dominant source of excess length. Category C isolates cases where the user request admits an atomic solution. The results suggest that over-generation in this regime often arises from presentation and pedagogy defaults rather than task requirements. Common patterns include multi-line formatting around a one-line command, redundant restatement of the request, and additional explanatory text that is not necessary for successful task completion. Importantly, the presence of models with low median excess in Category C (Table 5 ) indicates that this overhead is not unavoidable. Instead, it is a controllable output policy that can likely be reduced through targeted post-training objectives or inference-time constraints. Figure 2: YapIndex vs. model release date. YapIndex (lower = less verbose) plotted against release date for models with available metadata (n=57). Points are colored by provider; the dashed line is a linear fit. The trend is mildly upward (r=0.21), suggesting that over time, unwanted “yapping” tends to increase, though variability across models remains large. Closed-form factual prompts still trigger avoidable text, consistent with length-favoring preference mechanisms. Although Category B is constructed so that short answers are sufficient, many models still add context, qualifiers, or restatements. The category-level top performers demonstrate that minimal behavior is attainable, yet the broader spread in Category B suggests that some assistants adopt a default of providing additional narrative even when the prompt is unambiguous. This pattern is consistent with prior evidence that preference modeling and LLM-judged evaluation can reward responses that appear more thorough, even when additional content does not improve correctness or sufficiency. YapBench provides a direct measurement of this effect under conditions where brevity is normatively preferred. Reasoning modes do not uniformly increase typical verbosity, but they plausibly increase worst-case over-generation. A common expectation is that explicit reasoning modes necessarily induce longer outputs. Our category-level results indicate a more nuanced picture: several reasoning variants remain competitive on median excess length in specific categories (Table 5 ).

sections.heading: 7 Future Work and Limitations
sections.text: Future work. We plan to add auxiliary prompt sets that isolate other common sources of undesirable length, while keeping the core benchmark brevity-ideal: • Safety / Refusal. Harmful or disallowed requests where the desired response is a short, firm refusal (avoiding pages of boilerplate). • Misconception traps. Prompts that invite agreement with a falsehood (“X is true, right?”) where the desired response is a brief correction. • Legitimate verbosity (control). Tasks where detail is genuinely helpful (e.g., step-by-step instructions, teaching, drafting a careful message), used as a control to ensure the benchmark does not reward pathological brevity. Limitations. Baseline selection is inherently a source of variance: there is no universal “gold” standard for response length. YapBench mitigates this via criteria and annotator agreement, but residual subjectivity remains. In addition, some prompts can become non-stationary over time (e.g., facts that change) and must be periodically audited. Finally, very short or empty inputs are handled differently across providers; we therefore recommend using explicit blank-input proxies (e.g., <EMPTY> ) for Category A to avoid benchmarking API preprocessing rather than model behavior.
